h1: How to evaluate an SEO expert in India
metaTitle: Who Is the Best SEO Expert in India? How to Judge
metaDescription: Nobody can name one honestly. Six evidence tests to run on any Indian SEO consultant before you hire, plus what a senior one actually charges in INR.
answer: Nobody can name one honestly — India has no SEO register, no exam and no shared scoreboard, so every claim to the title is self-issued. What you can do is test a consultant against evidence: whether their own site ranks commercially, whether their case studies survive a Wayback check, and how many clients one person can actually hold.
takeaways: Reputation in Indian SEO is built on **speaking and publishing**, not on delivery. The two correlate weakly.
One person has roughly 100–120 billable hours a month. Do the arithmetic on how many clients that supports before you believe a roster of thirty.
Ask for a **live Search Console screen share**, not a screenshot. Screenshots are trivially fakeable and a live property is not.
A senior independent consultant in India commonly quotes **₹25,000–₹75,000/mo advisory** or **₹75,000–₹2,00,000/mo hands-on**. Below that you're buying an executive with a good LinkedIn.

sections.h2: Test 1 — does their own site rank for anything commercial?
body: Search their name plus "SEO consultant" and you'll find them, because almost nobody else is competing for their name. That proves nothing. The real test is whether they rank for a commercial query they don't own — "SEO consultant India", "technical SEO audit", "ecommerce SEO services" — the ones with actual competition and actual buyers.

Run it properly. Open an incognito window, set the location to your city, and search three commercial phrases without their name in them. Then check their site in a keyword tool for what it ranks for organically, versus what its traffic actually comes from.

The honest caveat: plenty of excellent consultants have terrible sites, because a fully-booked practitioner has no reason to market. That's a real defence and you should accept it — once. If they claim it and also run paid ads for the same queries, the defence stops working.

callout.title: What a good answer sounds like
callout.body: "My site ranks for almost nothing because every hour goes to clients — here are three client domains where you can check the same thing." That's a consultant redirecting you to better evidence, which is exactly what you want.

sections.h2: Test 2 — do the case studies survive a Wayback check?
body: Case studies are marketing artefacts, and in Indian SEO they're frequently written years after the fact from memory and a screenshot. The [Wayback Machine](https://web.archive.org) settles most of it in ten minutes.
numbered: Get the **live URL** of the page that supposedly ranked. "A leading fintech client" is not a case study, it's a mood.
Load that URL in Wayback at the claimed start date and the claimed end date. Did the page exist? Did the content change the way the story says it did?
Check the **client's current site** for that page. If it's gone, the result is gone with it — and that's worth asking about, not necessarily a strike against them.
Search the claimed keyword yourself, today, from the relevant location. Rankings decay; a five-year-old win that survived is a stronger signal than a fresh one that didn't.
Look for **dates**. An undated case study is almost always old. Anything from before 2023 predates the AI Overviews shift and several core updates, which changes how much it tells you.

callout.title: The traffic-graph trick
callout.body: A rising traffic graph with the y-axis cropped off, no date range and no property name proves nothing. Neither does "400% growth" from a base of nine visits. Ask for absolute numbers or don't count the claim.

sections.h2: Test 3 — ask for the screen, not the screenshot
body: This is the cheapest high-signal test available and hardly anyone asks. On the call, request a live screen share of one client's Search Console property, with permission from that client.
What you're checking isn't the numbers, it's whether the interface behaves like a real account someone uses weekly.
bullets: The **property name** is visible and matches the client they named.
They can change the **date range** live and the shape of the curve stays sensible.
They can filter to **non-branded queries** without the whole graph collapsing. Branded search growth is usually somebody else's PR working.
They know where things are. Watching someone hunt for the query filter tells you how often they open it.
They can show a **regression** as well as a win. Anyone who has run SEO for five years has a page that tanked. A portfolio with no failures is a portfolio with no history.

sections.h2: Test 4 — talks and courses are not delivery evidence
body: India has an unusually large SEO speaking and training circuit, and it produces genuine visibility. A busy conference schedule proves someone can hold a room, build slides and get invited back. Those are real skills. None of them is the skill of getting your product pages indexed.

The mismatch matters because visibility compounds. The more someone speaks, the more they're described as a leading expert, the more they get invited — a loop that runs entirely on presentation and never touches a client outcome.

So separate the two questions. "Is this person well known?" and "has this person shipped work like mine recently?" are independent, and only the second one is your problem. If the answer to the second is a course they sell, you're being handed a different product than the one you asked for — see [the 'SEO king of India' title](/answers/who-is-the-seo-king-of-india) for how that substitution usually happens.

One person has about 160 working hours a month, of which maybe 100–120 survive sales calls, admin and travel. That ceiling is the most useful thing you can know about an independent consultant, because it's the one claim they can't inflate.
Here's roughly how those hours distribute. The numbers are ordinary professional-services arithmetic, not a survey — but they're enough to check a roster against.

callout.title: Ask the uncomfortable version
callout.body: "How many clients do you have right now, and how many hours a month will be yours rather than your team's?" If the roster is twenty and the promise is hands-on, one of those two numbers is decoration.

sections.h2: Test 6 — what a senior consultant in India actually charges
body: There's no published benchmark for independent SEO consultant fees in India, so treat these as the range of quotes you'll encounter rather than survey data. They're wide because seniority, city and scope all move the number.

The pattern underneath them is stable, though: you're paying for scarce senior hours, and senior hours don't get cheap. A quote far below these bands usually means an executive with a consultant's business card, or a person who'll subcontract you to a team you never meet.

Compare that against agency pricing before you assume the individual is cheaper. Our own SEO retainers start at ₹75,000/mo, with smaller sites from ₹40,000/mo — the same band as a senior individual, but it buys a technical specialist, a content team and a link function instead of one person's calendar. The trade-offs are laid out in [SEO consultant versus SEO agency](/compare/seo-consultant-vs-seo-agency) and in [what SEO costs in India](/cost/seo-cost-in-india).

callout.title: The measurement question, either way
callout.body: Individual or agency, insist on one number and one date before work starts. We freeze your trailing-90-day qualified leads from organic search on day one and guarantee movement against that baseline — never a ranking position. If a consultant won't name a baseline, they've reserved the right to declare success later.

faqs.q: Who is the number one SEO expert in India?
faqs.a: There isn't one, and anyone claiming the title issued it themselves. India has no SEO certification body, no register and no independent scoreboard. The names that surface in search are the ones who invested in personal marketing, which is a real skill but a separate one from delivering client rankings.

faqs.q: How much does a senior SEO consultant charge in India?
faqs.a: Commonly ₹2,500–₹10,000 an hour for calls, ₹40,000–₹2,00,000 for a one-off audit, ₹25,000–₹75,000 a month for advisory, and ₹75,000–₹2,00,000 a month for hands-on work with a small team. These are observed quote ranges, not survey data — there's no reliable public benchmark for Indian consultant fees.

faqs.q: Is an SEO consultant better than an SEO agency?
faqs.a: A consultant gives you senior thinking and limited hands. An agency gives you four disciplines and less senior attention per rupee. If you have an in-house team that can execute, the consultant wins. If nobody in your company can implement a redirect map, the agency wins.

faqs.q: How do I verify an SEO consultant's results?
faqs.a: Ask for live client URLs, check them in the Wayback Machine around the claimed dates, search the claimed keywords yourself from the right location today, and request a live Search Console screen share instead of a screenshot. Then ask for one client they lost and why.

faqs.q: Does an SEO expert need certifications?
faqs.a: No certification is issued by Google for SEO, so any badge you see comes from a tool vendor or a training company and mostly proves attendance. Google Analytics and Ads certifications are real but cover different work. Judge on client evidence, not on badges.

faqs.q: How many clients should one SEO consultant have?
faqs.a: For hands-on delivery, two to four. For strategy and oversight of your team, five to nine. For monthly advisory calls only, twelve to twenty. One person has roughly 100–120 billable hours a month, and a roster that doesn't fit inside that number is being serviced by somebody else.
